Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- The patient presents with acute onset watery diarrhea (6–7 times/day), crampy left lower abdominal pain, initial vomiting (resolved), subjective fever at onset (now afebrile), and mild weakness/shakiness. Symptoms began after eating takeaway food; only one family member had transient vomiting without diarrhea.
- Clinical impression is consistent with acute gastroenteritis, likely foodborne in origin; viral or bacterial causes possible.
- No evidence of blood in stool or vomit; able to maintain hydration; no signs of severe dehydration or systemic illness.
- No indication for antibiotics at this stage.
- Advised conservative management (oral rehydration, rest, paracetamol for fever/discomfort).
- If symptoms persist beyond 3–4 more days, or worsen, stool testing and further evaluation to be considered.

Management Plan
- Conservative management recommended.
  - Maintain adequate hydration (oral fluids; Dioralyte/oral rehydration solution suggested).
  - Paracetamol for fever/discomfort (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Advise time off work for 2–3 days to allow for recovery.
  - Return for review if symptoms are not improving in 3–4 days or if condition worsens.
- No antibiotics prescribed.
- Stool testing to be considered if symptoms persist.

- Pathology tests as above:  Consider stool tests if persistent symptoms.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Acute gastroenteritis (viral or bacterial, foodborne infectious): High likelihood. Sudden onset after restaurant meal, watery diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, and self-limited symptoms strongly support this diagnosis.
- Food poisoning (bacterial, e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli): Moderate likelihood. Temporal association with takeaway meal and acute gastrointestinal symptoms.
- Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus, rotavirus): Moderate likelihood. Symptoms compatible, but spread among household contacts less prominent.
